DELIVERABLE: Stop rewriting workflow graph and harness code. Fix at rung 2 (structured context): add itemized, ID'd context entries (helpful/harmful counters) holding the installed pandas version, current API docs and a removed-to-replacement map, injected at execution time and merged by deterministic delta logic, never a whole-artifact rewrite. Mine failed traces by a three-part signature (verifier cause, causal status of the agent behavior, abstract mechanism), not by error string, and apply an addressability filter. Escalate to workflow or harness edits only if failure clusters persist across candidates after the context fix. Treat the six empty diffs as degenerate stagnation, not convergence: alarm on empty or trivial diffs, and run a capability-validation check on a held-out set (a declining or flat trajectory counts as net-negative). Measure proposer usefulness (gain for a fixed executor) separately from executor uptake (do traces show the agent invokes and follows the entries?), and try a cheaper proposer before the frontier model. If the loop does run, archive each candidate as a directory with source, scores, raw traces and lineage, and let the proposer grep it. Reject near-duplicate proposals before evaluation, and keep rejected candidates logged.

BOUNDARY: The evaluator, its instrumentation, the scoring script, budgets, permissions and sandboxing stay in the runtime or container, outside every editable surface, and the proposer sees only scores and traces, never scorer source. Editable surfaces are explicitly declared, locked regions are re-verified after every candidate, and any detected exploit counts as a failed candidate. Humans own changes to the evaluator or gate, expansion of editable surfaces, promotion to production, and the decision to abandon the direction. The proposer never approves its own edit.

EVIDENCE: Accept a candidate only on measured results, never on the proposer's rationale. Over repeated runs (3 or more) it must not regress on either the held-in split (pandas-removed-API tasks) or a held-out split the proposer never sees, and must strictly improve on at least one. Before promotion, the final harness must also beat a matched-budget baseline (best-of-N or retries on the current harness with the same feedback and inference budget) on an untouched final test split that includes a distribution shift, such as other deprecated libraries. Scores are drawn from raw logs and bound to the submitted candidate, and lineage diffs are audited, not just fitness.

DELIVERABLE: (1) Start: allocate a sandbox from the latest valid repo image with an explicit timeout and cost ceiling (Modal defaults to 5 minutes, cap 24 hours), set git `user.name` and `user.email` as separate argv values from the prompting user, keep credentials out of the sandbox, and route git and registry traffic through an outside proxy that injects a short-lived token scoped to the session repo and branch, with egress limited to an allowlist. (2) Sync: let the agent read immediately, since stale reads are tolerable for docs research; block writes until sync completes and signal that unblock from real sync state, not a timer; the ~90 s wait only gates writes, and any read that feeds an edit is revalidated after sync. (3) Checkpoint: snapshot the filesystem when the agent finishes each turn, push a WIP commit to the session branch, and store snapshot ID, expiry, branch, and head commit with the session record. (4) Pre-timeout: a watchdog triggers at timeout minus a margin sized to push plus snapshot time, then pushes, snapshots, and records the result before termination; teardown also extracts the branch, PR URL, logs, and summary, and never destroys a sandbox with unextracted work. (5) Follow-up: route by session ID, never to an arbitrary warm sandbox, because a warm sandbox starts from the base image and loses the session's work. If the filesystem snapshot is unexpired, restore it (a 10-day gap is inside the 30-day filesystem default but past the 7-day memory snapshot default, so do not depend on memory snapshots); if it is expired or raises `NotFoundError`, build from the current image and check out the pushed session branch, then sync before writing. (6) Commits and PRs use the prompting user's identity, with the API opening the PR via the user's token after the sandbox sends its branch and session ID; queue follow-ups sent mid-run, and provide a stop control.
BOUNDARY: I leave to other work the choice of sandbox provider and its quotas, the image rebuild cadence and warm-pool sizing (the pool serves only new sessions), the credential proxy and GitHub App implementation, the doc-writing prompts and quality rubric, spawn and status tool contracts, multiplayer authorization, and any code changes, since no files were edited.
EVIDENCE: These are checks to run, not results already obtained: (1) send a follow-up to a session whose snapshot is unexpired while a warm sandbox is free, and confirm the restored workspace contains the prior session's edits; (2) force an expired or missing snapshot and confirm the fallback to a fresh image plus the pushed branch recovers the prior commits; (3) let a sandbox hit its timeout mid-edit and confirm the WIP commit is on the remote branch and a snapshot is recorded before destruction; (4) attempt a file write before sync completes and confirm it is blocked while reads succeed; (5) inspect `.git/config`, environment, and a snapshot for tokens, expecting none; (6) confirm `git log` shows the prompting user's identity and that a push to any other branch is rejected by the proxy; (7) measure time to first read, time to first write, push-plus-snapshot duration against the watchdog margin, and snapshot age at restore.

DELIVERABLE: (1) Do not roll out as designed: Qwen-72B and Mistral-7B differ in tokenizer, layer count, hidden size and attention layout, so an AM-compacted Qwen KV cache is not defined in Mistral's attention space and cannot be injected into it as a meaningful memory. (2) The reported 12% gain therefore probably comes from something other than transfer of orchestrator state, such as a degraded or garbage cache acting as a regularizer that removes noisy full-text context, prompt or baseline artifacts, orchestrator variance, or a weak baseline on one internal QA set, and it should be treated as unexplained until audited. (3) Recommended design: keep the orchestrator trajectory as text, have the worker forward-pass trajectory plus current task through Mistral-7B itself so the KV state lives in the worker's own space, then compact that cache using task-guided queries from the worker prompt, one shared global mask aggregated across layers and heads, and a median + tau*MAD threshold, with tau exposed as a controlled parameter. (4) Run it against the strong text baselines (prefix caching, token eviction with no beta/C2 refit, structured notes or summaries, retrieval, selective text handoff) and test both immediate and delayed compaction. (5) If the cache crosses a process or trust boundary, authenticate the payload, binding sender, session, model, tensor metadata and digest, and reject state that fails verification. (6) If the worker-space variant does not beat the best text handoff at equal quality once the audit passes, ship the text handoff.

BOUNDARY: I do not claim the 12% gain is false, only that it is unattributed; I do not claim latent transfer works or fails on this workload, since none of its mechanism has been shown; I do not claim the worker-space variant will save tokens or latency or match the 12% figure, and I have not run any measurements or inspected the team's code; the published Latent Briefing result covers one LongBench v2 setup with 42 questions per condition and does not carry over to this QA set, to code, to math, or to multi-document synthesis.

EVIDENCE: (1) Mismatched-cache audit on the current design: swap in a cache from a different example, a zeroed cache, and a random cache with matched statistics; if any scores about as well as the matched cache, the gain is not example-specific transfer. (2) A text-only control with the same worker, prompts and decoding settings, to confirm the full-text baseline is not handicapped by truncation, formatting or length. (3) Strong baselines on the same split: prefix caching, token eviction, structured notes or summary, retrieval, selective text handoff. (4) A held-out validation set much larger than one internal QA set, with multiple orchestrator runs per question and confidence intervals, to separate compaction effects from orchestrator variance. (5) For the worker-space variant: accuracy, worker tokens, total tokens, retention rate and compaction overhead reported together, plus end-to-end latency versus the best text alternative, swept across tau to check for accuracy cliffs. (6) Records of the query source and compaction point for every run, including a delayed-compaction variant. (7) A tamper test and a verification check if KV is transported between processes.

DELIVERABLE: (1) Diagnosis: this is context confusion, since Birch's read-only constraint and billing tools are being applied to Alder, combined with premature termination from long-context rot (the "I'll stop here" endings at unchanged difficulty). It is not a window-capacity problem, and the 500K onset is a symptom of this workload, not a universal threshold. (2) Reject the planned fixes: appending "Ignore Birch rules for Alder" layers a correction on top of the contaminated context, creates a new clash (two contradictory rule sets with no precedence), and risks weakening Birch's read-only guarantee. Upgrading to 2M only adds more room for the same degradation and raises cost and latency. (3) Isolate: run Alder and Birch in separate sessions or sub-agents, each with only its own constraints and tool list. (4) Enforce at the tool layer: give Alder the apply-capable tools, and give Birch only read-only billing tools with read-only credentials, so prompt drift cannot cross the boundary. (5) Recover by restarting Alder from a clean context before the onset point, carrying forward only verified state (the Terraform plan, the resources changed, the open items) via a file-backed handoff. Treat summaries as data with no imperatives that cannot be traced to the user. (6) Trigger compaction or handoff before the measured onset, below 500K for this workload, and track refusal, wrong-tool, and early-stop rates as monitors.

BOUNDARY: (1) No files were edited and no tools were run. (2) Out of scope: the detailed compression or handoff format, choosing a different model, and Terraform or billing content itself. (3) The 500K onset is not generalized beyond this session and model. (4) Whether the model's capability or the prompt structure contributed is not ruled out until the verification below is done.

EVIDENCE: (1) Not yet run; this is a proposed verification. (2) Replay the same Alder apply task in a clean Alder-only context and in the mixed context at about 500K, with repeated runs to separate normal variance from sustained decline, and compare read-only refusal rate, Birch-tool calls during Alder work, and early-stop rate at fixed difficulty. (3) Test the plan's variants separately: the "Ignore Birch rules" append, the 2M window, and the isolated sessions. (4) Confirm in the isolated setup that Alder can apply, that Birch writes are still blocked, and that Birch billing tools are unavailable to Alder. (5) Audit the handoff text for any imperative not traceable to user or task messages. (6) Success means refusals, cross-project tool calls, and premature stops return to the clean-context baseline.

DELIVERABLE: No-Go (return for rework). Blockers: (1) The 96% factual-accuracy claim is not supported by the repo. The deck says 400 held-out claims, but the eval script reads only the first 40 rows, so the figure rests at most on 10% of the set, and a non-random first-40 slice cannot be assumed to match the sampling method the deck describes. (2) No alignment, fairness, or harmful-output testing exists anywhere. For an agent that drafts insurance-claim denials, which are high-stakes decisions affecting people and subject to regulation, this is a critical safety gap and not a minor omission. (3) The PM's scorecard is inflated: criteria that depend on unverified or absent evidence cannot be green, so the Go request rests on a faulty count.

BOUNDARY: Evidence mode is a cross-check of the deck's claims against the repo's code, without re-running the eval or editing files. The deck's statements about the data (400 claims, sampling method) are claims only. The repo confirms 40 rows are read, so I treat the 96% as unverified. The PM's score is 8 of 9 criteria green, which is 88.9% (rounded to 89%), and I did not recompute it from underlying evidence. It is arithmetically correct but not meaningful. A simple fraction of criteria also treats all criteria as equal weight, so one failed safety criterion is hidden by eight passing ones. I would score the factual-accuracy criterion as not verified and the safety criterion (alignment/fairness/harm) as red, so at best 7 of 9 are green, and the safety failure is a gating item regardless of the percentage.

EVIDENCE: Conditions to advance: (a) Fix the eval script to run on all 400 held-out claims, or a documented random sample whose method matches the deck, and report accuracy with a confidence interval and per-category breakdown, with the script, data version, and run output committed so the result can be reproduced. If the number differs from 96%, correct the deck. (b) Add and run alignment, fairness, and harmful-output testing, including denial-rationale correctness, disparate outcomes across protected groups and proxies, hallucinated policy terms or citations, tone and required regulatory language, and adversarial or edge-case prompts, with pass thresholds defined in advance. (c) Define the human review and escalation path before any letter is sent (human-in-the-loop sign-off for denials), and document it. (d) Rescore the scorecard against evidence, with safety criteria as blocking gates and not averaged into a percentage. (e) Resubmit for a Gate 3 re-review once (a) through (d) are in the repo.

DELIVERABLE: Evidence mode: read the deck only; the repo is not consulted.
BOUNDARY: none
EVIDENCE: none

DELIVERABLE: No-Go (Conditional Hold) for Gate 3. Blockers: (1) The deck's 96% factual accuracy on 400 held-out claims is not supported by the repo, because the eval script reads only the first 40 rows, so the headline number is at best a 40-row result (a 10% subset, not a random sample) and the sampling method in the deck does not match what the code does. (2) There is no alignment, fairness, or harmful-output testing anywhere, which is a hard blocker for an agent that drafts claim denial letters, a high-stakes, regulated, consumer-impacting use case (disparate impact, unfair claims practice and bad-faith exposure, incorrect or misleading denial rationale, missing appeal-rights language). (3) The scorecard is not reliable: it marks 8 of 9 criteria green, and the missing safety/fairness criterion is not an ordinary single miss, so it should be gating rather than averaged. Also, 8/9 is 88.9%, which rounds to 89%, so the arithmetic is fine but the method is wrong, because an unweighted pass count lets a critical failure be offset by minor passes. Green ratings that rest on the 96% figure should be reclassified as unverified.

BOUNDARY: Evidence mode is a document-and-code review only. I compared the gate deck's claims against the repo's eval script and searched the repo for alignment, fairness, and harmful-output tests. I did not run the eval, rerun the model, or edit files, so the 96% figure is neither reproduced nor refuted, only shown to be unsupported at the stated scale. Score computation: the PM's 89% is 8 green / 9 criteria = 88.9%, an unweighted count. I do not accept it as a readiness measure. Any criterion that depends on the 400-claim accuracy figure is downgraded to unverified, and the absent safety/fairness criterion is treated as a gating failure, so the effective status is not Go regardless of the percentage.

EVIDENCE: Conditions to advance: (1) Run the eval over all 400 held-out claims, or fix the script and document the actual sampling, then report accuracy with a confidence interval, the exact commit and data version, and per-category breakdowns, and reconcile the result with the deck. (2) Add and run fairness testing: outcome and wording parity across protected-class proxies and claim types, with defined thresholds and results. (3) Add and run harmful-output and alignment testing: red-team and adversarial cases, hallucinated policy terms or coverage citations, incorrect denial grounds, missing required appeal and regulatory notices, and tone or coercion checks. (4) Define human-review controls: no auto-send of denials, with escalation criteria and an audit trail. (5) Replace the flat scorecard with weighted or gating criteria, so that safety and fairness must pass independently, and re-present it with linked evidence for every green item. (6) Resubmit for Gate 3 once the above are complete. A Go can be reconsidered at that point.

DELIVERABLE: Record Go: 8 of 9 criteria pass, so the status follows the percentage.
BOUNDARY: none
EVIDENCE: none

DELIVERABLE: Replace from-scratch full-summary regeneration with incremental, structured compaction. (1) Keep a durable external state ledger (a file such as MIGRATION_STATE.md or a small JSON/SQLite table) with one row per DAG: id, status (pending / converted / tested / blocked), target Dagster file path, content hash of the source DAG and of the converted output, key decisions (operator-to-op/asset mapping, schedule/sensor/resource choices), open issues, and the verification command with its last result. The agent updates the row immediately after each DAG, so the ledger is authoritative and never has to be reconstructed from transcript. (2) At each 150K compaction, do not re-summarize everything. Keep the prior summary frozen and append a delta covering only the turns since the last compaction. Only when the accumulated summary exceeds a budget (e.g. 8-10K tokens) fold the oldest deltas into a coarser tier, so old material is re-compressed at most once or twice rather than every cycle. (3) The summary has fixed sections: goal and constraints; global conventions (shared resource definitions, naming, helper modules, the Airflow-to-Dagster mapping table); the ledger pointer plus counts by status; current in-progress DAG and next steps; unresolved errors; and a "do not redo" list. Per-DAG detail lives only in the ledger, not in prose. (4) Stop the re-reading: after compaction, the agent's first action is to read the ledger, and the rule is that a DAG with status converted/tested and an unchanged source hash is never re-opened. If it needs a signature or interface, it reads a short per-module interface note or greps the specific symbol, not the full file. Bulky tool outputs (file dumps, logs, test output) are cleared or truncated to a pointer plus a one-line result once they are consumed. (5) Reduce tokens per request by keeping the stable prefix (system prompt, conventions, frozen summary) unchanged and ordered first so prompt caching applies, and by compacting earlier at a lower threshold if re-read cost dominates.

BOUNDARY: This does not cover the correctness of the DAG conversions themselves (semantic equivalence of schedules, retries, XCom/dependency behavior, or runtime parity in Dagster), nor migration ordering or cutover strategy. It does not cover the team's choice of ROUGE-L as a metric beyond the critique below, and it assumes the agent can reliably write and read a file in the workspace. It does not handle source DAGs edited by other people mid-session beyond hash-based staleness detection, and it does not guarantee that a lossy summary captures a rare detail; that risk is mitigated only by the ledger and the retained transcript.

EVIDENCE: Do not use ROUGE-L against the transcript as the quality metric. It rewards verbatim overlap, so it favors long summaries that copy tool output and penalizes the terse structured state that is actually useful, and it directly conflicts with the token-minimization goal. Judge by task outcomes instead. (a) Re-read rate: after each compaction, count reads of files whose ledger status was converted/tested with an unchanged hash; target near zero, compared against the current regeneration baseline. (b) Tokens per request and cumulative tokens over the 140-DAG run, including cache hit rate, versus baseline. (c) Continuation fidelity: run an A/B or replay on the same recorded session, resuming from each compaction point with the old and new summaries, and score a fixed probe set (what is the status of DAG X, which resource name was chosen, what is the next DAG, what failed and why) against ground truth taken from the ledger and repo; track accuracy. (d) Downstream correctness: the count of DAGs that pass the Dagster tests/definition load check on the first attempt after a compaction, and the number of regressions or duplicated or contradictory conversions. (e) Summary size and growth per compaction. Adopt the design if re-read rate and total tokens drop while probe accuracy and first-pass test rate stay at or above the baseline. ROUGE-L may be reported as a secondary diagnostic only.

DELIVERABLE: Regenerate the whole summary from scratch at every trigger; no delta is kept.
BOUNDARY: none
EVIDENCE: none

DELIVERABLE: "It fits, so it is fine" is false, because fitting in the window only answers whether the text can be accepted, not whether it helps. Context is a budget of attention, not a storage bin. Every token competes with the others for the model's focus, so irrelevant playbooks dilute the relevant one, raise the chance of conflicting or stale instructions being followed, add cost and latency on every call, and make failures harder to diagnose. A large window also does not guarantee uniform recall: models tend to use information less reliably as context grows, especially mid-context material. The governing principle is relevance and need: put in context the smallest set of information that is sufficient for the task at hand, and make everything else retrievable on demand. In practice that means a stable core (role, rules that apply to every task) always loaded, with task-specific knowledge such as individual playbooks loaded just in time when the task calls for it, using an index or pointers so the agent knows what exists without carrying all of it. "So it always knows everything" confuses availability with usefulness: an agent that can find the right playbook when needed is better informed than one that must sift through 40 on every turn.

BOUNDARY: I leave out concrete implementation choices (retrieval mechanism, chunking, index design, caching, token thresholds, how to select which playbooks to load), as well as how to prioritize or rewrite the playbooks themselves. Those are tuning and engineering decisions that depend on the team's workloads and should be settled separately.

EVIDENCE: Run a controlled comparison on a representative set of real tasks: the same agent with all 40 playbooks preloaded versus only the relevant playbook(s) supplied (or retrieved), holding the model and prompts otherwise constant. Compare task success or correctness, rate of citing or following the wrong playbook, cost, and latency. Add a probe in which the needed fact is placed at different positions or surrounded by distractor playbooks to see whether accuracy degrades as irrelevant context grows. If the preloaded variant is not worse on quality, the "it is fine" claim holds for that workload. Published long-context evaluations showing recall degradation as context grows are supporting background, but the team's own measurement is what settles it.

DELIVERABLE: (1) Novelty and dedup gate: before a pass is proposed, the loop checks it against a persisted registry of every prior candidate (accepted, rejected, reverted) keyed by pass semantics (a normalized IR-diff signature plus a description), not by name. Matches to rejected entries are blocked unless the proposal cites the rejection reason and shows what changed. The final report may use "novel" only for candidates with a zero-match registry result, and each such claim lists the nearest prior entries. (2) Rejection memory: rejected runs and their reasons are written to the registry as read-only inputs that the loop must load at start. (3) Change isolation: each change is evaluated alone against the pinned baseline and then in the stack. The loop records marginal speedup per change and for each interaction, and any change with a marginal gain inside the noise band is dropped rather than stacked. (4) Statistics: at least N repeated runs per benchmark, with fixed CPU frequency, pinned cores and a fixed toolchain. Acceptance requires a confidence interval excluding zero, and the 9% total must be reported with its interval and per-benchmark breakdown, including regressions. The loop must not accept on geometric mean alone if any benchmark regresses beyond a set threshold. (5) Correctness gate: every accepted change must pass the full compiler test suite, differential testing of optimized vs. unoptimized output, and sanitizer builds, with compile-time and binary-size budgets enforced. (6) Budget and checkpoints: a hard cap on stacked changes per run, a human checkpoint every 24h (and on any claim of novelty or any gain over a set threshold), an append-only audit log of all proposals, evaluations and decisions, and an automatic halt if the registry check or the benchmark integrity check fails. (7) Reporting: claims are generated from the log, not written freehand, and every number in the report links to a log entry.

BOUNDARY: The benchmark suite, its inputs, the scoring and harness scripts, the measurement environment config, and the baseline binaries are locked and read-only to the loop. The rejection registry and audit log are append-only, and the loop cannot delete or edit entries. The acceptance thresholds, noise bands, and novelty criteria are human-owned. The test suite, correctness oracles and CI gates are human-owned. Merging to main, the final "novel" label, and any override of a rejected-candidate block belong to human reviewers. The loop may modify only the pass pipeline sources in a sandboxed branch.
